source.title: CADENCE: A Cardiac Atom Dictionary for Interpretable Neural Concept Extraction from ECG Foundation Models
source.authors: Yi-Xuan Duan; Arjun Naik; Sadeer Al-Kindi; Weijing Qiu

page_placements.theme: Enlarging the dictionary adds dead, rare or low-sensitivity latents more than new concepts

record.tranche_reason: The study varies Layer-6 SAE dictionary size and reports that the count of phenotype-specific atoms does not increase with larger dictionaries. It does not directly match features across sizes or test whether their activations partition a coarse feature.
record.gate_note: The Layer-6 size grid reports phenotype-specific atom counts for selected dictionary sizes; these bear indirectly on whether larger dictionaries yield more specific features. The study does not report cross-size feature correspondences, input-set partitioning, or directional similarity. Other SAE results, including prediction and ablation results, do not test the splitting claim.
record.test_reason: The study applies a BatchTopK SAE to an ECG foundation model; it does not test feature splitting. Its only dictionary-size result is a Layer-6 hyperparameter grid (App. A.1, Fig. A2) reporting counts of phenotype-specific atoms. That count cannot show the effect splitting describes, which is a coarse feature replaced by finer features that cover its inputs and lie near its direction. The study does no cross-size feature matching, input-overlap analysis or decoder-direction comparison, and does not mention splitting or absorption. Towards Monosemanticity is cited only as general SAE background. The record's 'tests/T5' is therefore wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only the appendix grid. The authors' main conclusion is that a BatchTopK SAE decomposes a frozen 12-lead ECG foundation model into sparse atoms that align with clinical concepts better than raw neurons. They also report that sparse atom probes match or beat dense probes, and that atom-space geometry recovers physiological relations. Further claims: single-atom ablation selectively changes frozen readouts, LLM descriptions are validated, and results transfer to PTB-XL. The grid statement, that a larger F adds no specific atoms at this width, is a side remark justifying F=8192.
record.recipe_differences: Applies a BatchTopK SAE to ECG foundation-model activations; dictionary-size results use phenotype-specific atom counts rather than cross-size feature matching, input-set overlap, or directional similarity.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary size and sparsity are varied in the Layer-6 hyperparameter grid.

fits_no_version.finding: In a Layer-6 ECG-FM BatchTopK SAE at k=128, the count of phenotype-specific atoms is flat or falls as F grows (459, 458, 440 for F=8192, 16384, 32768). Dead-atom fraction rises at the same time (21%, 49%, 70%), and explained variance is flat (0.966 to 0.969).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small-width non-language backbones, enlarging the SAE dictionary mainly adds dead latents rather than more concept-specific latents; interpretability yield saturates.

record.problems: The dictionary-size comparison uses phenotype-specific atom count as a proxy for interpretability yield, not direct evidence of feature splitting or correspondence. The text provides no uncertainty estimates for these counts.
record.rows_left_out: No other size-grid values were reported in the text as numeric phenotype-specific atom counts. Other results do not measure the splitting claim.

untested.parts: All of it. No study of whether larger-dictionary atoms replace, partition or lie near smaller-dictionary atoms.
All of it. Only one small ECG backbone (6 layers, d=768) and its own SAEs.
All of it. The 'hierarchical' rhythm/phenotype/morphology levels are a taxonomy of atom types, not nested split families.
All of it. No parent/child latent firing analysis.
All of it. No cross-size decomposition of latents.
All of it. No comparison with other training objectives.

record.verdict_notes: The study never addresses feature splitting. The grid also includes F=4096 and other k values, which are shown only in Fig. A2 and not given numerically. Two aVR pre-QRS notch atoms (L6/1576, L6/7800) look redundant within one dictionary, but no cross-size analysis is done. The 'layered vocabulary' claim (rhythm, phenotype, morphology) is not evidence for V3's nested split families.

versions.untested_parts: Whether larger-dictionary features replace a particular smaller feature, cover roughly the same inputs in a partition, or point in nearby directions.

relation.reason: It does not test splitting. It cites Bricken et al. 2023 and Templeton et al. 2024 only as SAE references and never mentions feature splitting, so nothing fits better.

tranche.reason: The study applies a BatchTopK SAE to an ECG foundation model (CSFM). Its only dictionary-size result is a hyperparameter grid scored by counts of phenotype-specific atoms, which cannot show splitting. The text never discusses feature splitting.

source_check.notes: The App. A.1 grid covers F in {4096, 8192, 16384, 32768} and k in {32, 64, 128, 256}. The rows record only the k=128 slice, as selection values. The backbone is CSFM Tiny, not ECG-FM. The study never discusses feature splitting.

statements.correction: Backbone: CSFM (Cardiac Sensing FM), Tiny variant, Layer-6 residual stream (Table A2). At k=128 the phenotype-specific atom counts are 459, 458 and 440 for F=8192, 16384 and 32768, and the dead fraction is 21%, 49% and 70%. EV moves 0.966 to 0.969 as F grows 8x (F=4096 to 32768).
statements.problem: All numbers match App. A.1. But the statement names the backbone 'ECG-FM', the name of a different published model (McKeen et al. 2024, the study's ref [31]). The SAE is trained on CSFM.
